question.leadin: These men got the idea of flying from the bicycle shop they worked at.
question.text: Name these brothers, who invented the first airplane and successfully had a test flight near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina.
question.clue: With Glenn Curtiss, this group established a corporation that still exists today, which is headquartered in North Carolina.

swap.leadin: This policy was enforced by the Volstead Act.
swap.text: Name this policy, which banned the sale or prodution of alcoholic beverages in the United States between 1920 and 1933.
swap.clue: A hatchet was used in activism for this policy by Carrie Nation.

question.text: Susan B. Anthony fought for this amendment to the Constitution that legally granted women the right to vote.
question.clue: Specters of a new Force Bill were used by "antis" like Josephine Parker to argue against this legislation on racial grounds.

swap.text: The Atlanta Compromise was criticized as weak by W.E.B. Du Bois and other co-founders of this American civil rights organization. Thurgood Marshall represented this group in arguments before the Supreme Court, including Brown v. Board.
swap.answerHtml: NAACP (accept National Association for the Advancement of Colored People)
swap.clue: Ralph David Abernathy was first part of this group before he led the SCLC.

question.text: This man was President of Empire State, Incorporated during the skyscraper's construction. Nicknamed "The Happy Warrior," this man earlier served as governor of New York and was the first Catholic presidential nominee.
question.clue: In his only election as his party's candidate for president, he courted southerners by naming Arkansas senator Joseph Robinson as his running mate.

swap.leadin: President Warren G. Harding supported a bill introduced by Leonidas Dyer that wanted to make this act a federal felony.
swap.text: Name these punishments outside the law that were often applied by mobs. Ida B. Wells described her lifelong campaigns against these events in Crusade for Justice.
swap.clue: Ida B. Wells published an expose on this action, which was chronicled by the Department of Records and Archives at the Tuskegee Institute.

question.leadin: Answer the following about the Ku Klux Klan.
question.text: This 1915 film by D.W. Griffith dramatized the foundation of the Ku Klux Klan and was the first film to be aired in the White House.
question.clue: The mulatto Lydia Brown causes the disastrous sexual attraction of a prominent senator in one scene, while later Gus forces Flora to jump off a cliff after she rejects his marriage proposal.

swap.text: This act was passed in 1919 to enforce the Eighteenth Amendment. As a result, gangs took over production and distribution of alcoholic beverages.
swap.clue: It was sponsored by the chair of the House Judiciary Committee, a congressman from Minnesota, and it gave power of enforcement to the Commissioner of Internal Revenue.

question.text: Before becoming executive director, Wilkins spent fifteen years editing this NAACP magazine, previously overseen by W.E.B. DuBois and Jessie Fauset.
question.clue: It begins by noting that the "summer soldier" and the "sunshine patriot" will shrink from facing the title challenge, in which "these are the times that try men's souls."

swap.text: This Irish-born co-founder of the IWW organized a march of silk workers dubbed the "Children's Crusade," and was called "the most dangerous woman in America" for her work with the United Mine Workers.
swap.clue: To protest the use of child labor in Pennsylvania silk mills, this activist marched young mill workers 120 miles to the house of Teddy Roosevelt.

question.leadin: This president declared that "the chief business of the American people is business."
question.text: Name this president who promoted laissez-faire economics despite supporting government intervention as governor of Massachusetts. This "silent" president vetoed the McNary-Haugen Farm Relief Bill while in office.

swap.leadin: Answer these questions about a monumental effort.
swap.text: This secretary of state under presidents McKinley and Roosevelt signed a treaty with Lord Pauncefote of Britain granting the U.S. exclusive rights to build the canal. In that position he also formulated the Open Door policy to treat with China.
swap.clue: This man, who got his start as Lincoln's personal secretary, negotiated the treaty to end the war with Spain, and negotiated the treaty to build the Panama Canal. He also established the "Open Door" policy with China.

question.text: After being reelected to the House of Representatives, Victor Berger was denied his seat when he was convicted under this act. The phrase "clear and present danger" originated in a case regarding this act.
question.clue: This 1917 legislation that Daniel Ellsberg was accused of violating for stealing and leaking the Pentagon Papers.

swap.text: Supporters of this anarchist put a bomb under Palmer's porch and were alleged to have committed the 1920 Wall Street Bombing. This man founded and edited the newspaper The Subversive Chronicle.
swap.clue: This associate of Mike Boda formed a group that committed the crime that led to the arrest of Andrea Salsedo, who died from falling out of a window on 15 Park Row in New York.

question.leadin: When he was shot, this man told police "you stick to your trade, I'll stick to mine" and refused to name his killer.
question.text: Name this Jewish-American mobster known as the "Brain." He helped fix the 1919 World Series, was the inspiration for Meyer Wolfsheim in The Great Gatsby, and may have been killed by Dutch Schultz.
question.clue: The alleged mastermind behind the fix was this Jewish mobster and bootlegger who mentored Lucky Luciano and was killed in New York City in 1928 over poker debts.

swap.text: This muckraker and author of the The Shame of the Cities was sympathetic to the McNamaras' cause but claimed they confessed their guilt in the bombing to him. He was a staunch supporter of the Soviet Revolution.
swap.clue: With Ray Baker and Ida Tarbell, he founded American Magazine as a platform for his trademark style of journalism, and his investigations into municipal corruption were collected as The Struggle for Self-Government and The Shame of the Cities. .

question.text: This founder of the IWW known as "Big Bill" had far better luck in his trial, in which he was acquitted of ordering the murder of former Idaho governor Frank Steunenberg.
question.clue: This labor leader and Secretary-Treasurer of the Western Federation of Miners, who was defended by Clarence Darrow when he was accused of murdering Frank Steunenberg.

swap.leadin: One of these cases, Dooley v. United States, upheld Congress' power to tax exports to Puerto Rico, although tariffs on imports were overturned in another of these cases, De Lima v. Bidwell.
swap.text: Identify this name given to a series of early 20th century cases that decided matters like whether the Bill of Rights applied to overseas territories controlled by the United States.
swap.clue: The acquisition of territories from Spain as a result of the treaty led directly to these series of Supreme Court cases, which addressed the question "does the Constitution follow the flag?"

question.leadin: Answer the following about American pietism around the turn of the 20th century, FTPE.
question.text: This pastor of the Central Congregational Church in Topeka and leader of the Social Gospel is best known for his sermon stories which were novelized as the popular book In His Steps.

swap.text: This awesome jew, who would later Replace Holmes on the Supreme Court, wrote the opinion in Pfalsgraf. He also wrote a notable concurrence to Schechter Poultry and the book Paradoxes of Legal Science.
swap.clue: After eighteen years of revolutionizing many areas of the common law from the New York Court of Appeals, this man was appointed to the Supreme Court by Herbert Hoover.
